extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, mathematical educators, and mathematical communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how mathematicians should do, present, check, and value mathematical work — focusing on proofs, explanation, social processes, and the goal of advancing human understanding. Emphasizes exposition, audience-tailoring, infrastructure, and the social verification of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance human understanding of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The central aim of mathematical work is to advance human understanding of mathematics, not merely to produce theorems or formal derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work by whether it enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics. Distinguish 'knowledge that a theorem is true' from 'human understanding of why it is true' (example: Appel–Haken 4-color proof evoked desire for human-understandable proof). Avoid producing collections of answers (e.g., printing 10,000 primes) in lieu of insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey multiple conceptualizations and mental models
rubrics_metrics.description: Good mathematical exposition presents the diverse ways people think about a concept (intuition, geometric picture, symbolic rules, logical definition, approximation, rate, microscopic view, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide several complementary ways to understand a concept (Thurston's list for the derivative: infinitesimal, symbolic, logical, geometric, rate, approximation, microscopic). Avoid collapsing these into only formal definitions; 'unless great efforts are made to maintain the tone and flavor of the original human insights, the differences start to evaporate.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-sensitive exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs, talks, and papers must be addressed to and adapted for their intended audience; the same idea may require very different presentation for different groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging clarity or completeness, consider intended audience and subfield knowledge. In talks and papers, state prerequisites and context; anticipate that an idea that takes two minutes for insiders may take an hour for others. Avoid one-size-fits-all presentations (anti-pattern: colloquium speakers who plunge into technical details and lose most listeners in first 5 minutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and document background infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable work includes creating the background, definitions, names, and unifying concepts that make ideas accessible and reusable by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess expository/infrastructural work (definitions, motivating examples, new terminology like 'group' or 'manifold') as important contributions. Provide background, motivations, and explanations to lower entry barriers; avoid terse conventional styles that assume shared, unstated cultural knowledge (example: foliation papers that raised a high entry barrier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value diverse contributions beyond theorem-credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit systems that reward only theorem-proving undervalue exposition, infrastructure-building, mentoring, and social work that advance mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating careers or work, include non-theorem activities (writing accessible notes, teaching, building research communities, software/videos). Recognize team/ecological effects: many advances depend on collective contributions, not only the individual who states a final theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize human-understandable proofs (while maintaining standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be clear, simple, and humanly understandable; formal completeness is a different and complementary aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect careful proofs that will stand scrutiny, but value clarity that makes potential weaknesses easy to detect. Do not conflate human-checkable arguments with lax standards; rather, make arguments explicit enough for critical examination. Formal, fully machine-checked proofs are desirable but currently often impractical for entire bodies of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on social verification and communal standards of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical validity largely depends on social processes: expert scrutiny, exchange of ideas, and community consensus, not solely on immediately available formal derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a proof, consider the community's acceptance process (examples: Andrew Wiles's proof being accepted at high level before all details were checked). Experts are generally good at detecting potential weaknesses even without full formal checking. Encourage dialogue and checking rather than blind reliance on paperwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve intuition and human insights in formalization
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating informal ideas into formal definitions and proofs, preserve the motivating human insights and intuitive structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing documentation that strips out the original tone/flavor of insight; include explanations, metaphors, and motivating remarks so that formalism does not obscure meaning. Anti-pattern: purely formal write-ups that leave readers without the mental infrastructure to reconstruct the ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage multimodal communication channels in oral exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective oral communication uses gestures, diagrams, examples, and two-way interaction in addition to formal language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design talks and seminars to be interactive and rich in visual/gestural material; encourage audience questions and adapt to their needs. Avoid rigid, pre-set outlines that prevent addressing listener confusion; recognize one-on-one and small-group channels convey more than formal symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make intended prerequisites and scope explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers and speakers should state what background and infrastructure are assumed so readers can judge how much expansion is needed to understand the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label parts of proofs or expositions according to the prerequisite knowledge required. Be explicit about which audience each portion is addressed to (insider/neighboring subfield/general mathematical public). This helps evaluate whether a paper or talk successfully communicates to its target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support formalization efforts while recognizing practical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer formalization of mathematics is an important, worthwhile project that will yield clarity and tools, but it is presently incomplete and impractical to expect full formalization of all mathematical literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and assess work that advances formal proof tools; judge formalization as complementary to human exposition rather than a wholesale replacement in the near term. Expect formal systems to teach simplification and clarifying structures over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to critique by filling gaps and correcting errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice includes later refinement: filling in gaps, correcting errors, and supplying more detailed scholarship when motivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate authors positively for making arguments easier to check and for supplying detail when weaknesses are pointed out. The community values responsiveness and the production of clearer, more reliable documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess teaching and evaluation by depth of understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational assessments should measure genuine understanding rather than only stimulus–response or rote procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design homework, tests, and grading scales to require conceptual grasp and use multiple representations/modes of thinking. Avoid setting problems or grading policies that reward only superficial procedural performance (anti-pattern: tests much easier than covered material, graded on scales needing little understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about foundational assumptions and their provisional nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundational frameworks (set theory choices, 'polite fictions') are often pragmatic and not uniquely determined; authors should state assumptions transparently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing generality or metaphysical claims, check whether foundational choices are declared and whether reliance on particular frameworks is noted. Do not penalize reasonable pragmatic choices, but encourage clarity about their role and limits (example: multiple set-theoretic 'mathematical universes').
